claims.text: A multi-fidelity machine-learning framework can integrate high-throughput phonon calculations with iterative experimental feedback.
The proposed framework will predict phonon-limited thermal conductivity at least 30% more accurately than conventional semi-empirical or single-fidelity methods.
The framework's advantage will arise from accounting for chemical disorder and short-range order.
High-entropy alloys can exhibit short-range ordering or chemical clustering over substantial temperature ranges.
Chemical disorder and short-range order increase phonon-scattering pathways.
Local lattice distortions caused by disorder reduce phonon mean free path.
Machine learning can correlate local distortions and compositional fluctuations with measured thermal transport.
Capturing atomistic scattering mechanisms will improve prediction of low thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The intended material scope is near-equimolar high-entropy alloys containing four to six principal elements.
As-cast or similarly homogenized forms provide optimal compositional uniformity.
Combining partial atomic-displacement data, local-environment descriptors, limited ab initio calculations, and targeted measurements will improve model fidelity.
Advanced computational and data-driven tools are useful for efficiently exploring the large compositional space of high-entropy alloys.
Temperatures from approximately 400 to 900 K are relevant to the proposed thermal-insulation application.
Maintaining single-phase or nearly single-phase conditions ensures that phonon scattering dominates thermal transport.
Current semi-empirical and high-throughput ab initio models do not fully capture short-range order or localized-displacement effects in compositionally complex alloys.
The approach is best suited to near-single-phase or moderate-phase-fraction high-entropy alloys in the four-to-six-element range.
Use outside the stated composition and temperature ranges may require additional calibration.
Large anisotropy or multiple complex phases may require additional training data and validation.
The model can be benchmarked against direct thermal-conductivity measurements over 400–900 K and against predictions from current methods.
Failure to achieve the stated 30% error improvement over current methods would refute the hypothesis.
